The election is over. What’s supposed to happen next for Congress?
The U.S. Capitol Building in Washington, D.C., on May 7, 2025 (Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom).
WASHINGTON — Voting ended Tuesday in this year’s midterm elections, leaving officials and volunteers counting tens of millions of ballots to determine which U.S. House and Senate candidates will take the oath of office in January.
The post-election process includes numerous steps and varying deadlines for when ballots have to be certified, since each state has different laws governing not only what happens on Election Day but what happens afterward.
Once local and state election officials wrap up their work, the process moves to Congress, which has its own rules and procedures. The Constitution also gives the House and Senate final say over whether to seat someone.
Here’s a look at what’s next and where issues could arise, aside from lawsuits that may be filed or already in progress.
When will there be official results?
Counting ballots and certifying the results takes at least a week in most states, often longer.
Kyle Yoder, research director at The Center for Election Innovation & Research, said that is exactly the type of deliberative process voters should want and expect. He also cautioned the results news organizations report in the hours and sometimes days after Nov. 3 aren’t final totals.
“Results aren’t official until every ballot has been counted by every eligible voter,” he said. “That process takes time, and when you sit back and think about it, you want it to take time because what we want is for that count to be correct, for it to be accurate, for it to be complete.”
Yoder added that the “biggest point of confusion that we run into when we’re talking to voters about all this is they think the results they’re seeing on their TV on election night are the final results.”
The Associated Press, which many news organizations look to for race calls, explains how its experts decide when to announce a winner and when to wait for more ballots to be counted. The Election Law Program, a collaborative effort between William & Mary Law School and the National Center for State Courts, has timelines for the various state deadlines.
How long can states take to recount ballots?
After election officials certify the first count of ballots, especially close races can head into a recount. Some state laws require it automatically if the margin of victory is under a certain percentage. In other circumstances, specific people can request a recount, typically the runner-up, though some state laws allow voters or even political parties to request another count.
“In many states, election recounts, legal challenges to the results, etcetera, can only begin once results have been certified,” Yoder said. “So it is in the interest of politicians who may be saber-rattling to allow certification to happen, so that they can begin those recounts, legal challenges.”
States have various deadlines for how long those recounts can last. But they can drag on amid lawsuits and Congress has the authority in some cases to conduct its own recount.

James Alcorn, senior director of the Election Law Program at the William & Mary Law School, said “it depends” on the state law, but that statewide races are typically certified by a secretary of state or a state board of elections.

U.S. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York speaks to reporters at the U.S. Capitol on Oct. 3, 2023. (Photo by Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom)
WASHINGTON — U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries got one step closer to becoming the next speaker after Democrats delivered a sweeping victory in the midterm elections.
If elected by a majority of House members, Jeffries would make history as the first Black person to hold the gavel. The 56-year-old Brooklynite would lead Democrats’ charge against President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans’ policies, while pursuing an affordability and accountability-focused agenda.
Democrats are set to control both the House and Senate in the new Congress after a blue tsunami tore through the country on Election Day.
Jeffries — who’s represented the Empire State’s 8th Congressional District since 2013 — would have to navigate a challenging terrain that includes internal divisions in his caucus and a president all but certain to veto many of the party’s measures.
Jeffries would be the first Democratic speaker since Rep. Nancy Pelosi of California.
How hard to push Trump
Since Trump returned to office in January of last year, Jeffries, whom House Democrats elected as minority leader in late 2022, has stood at the forefront of Democrats’ pushback against the administration, a difficult project amid Republican control of both chambers of Congress and the presidency.
As that pushback ramps up under a Democratic House majority that has campaigned in part on holding the administration accountable, Jeffries will have to decide whether his party will seek to impeach Trump. That undertaking could compete with a slew of policy priorities on tap in the next Congress.
Trump was impeached twice in the House and acquitted both times in the Senate during his first term. Jeffries was one of the seven House impeachment managers during Trump’s first Senate impeachment trial in 2020.
Healthcare a top issue

Late last year, a friend in Seattle suggested we train for an Ironman 70.3 from opposite coasts. He did the runs, swims, and bike rides along the Pacific Ocean, and I followed suit along the Chesapeake Bay. We weren’t sure whether we’d meet in the middle for an organized event in Nebraska, or save on travel costs with an unofficial “Do-It-Yourself” approach in our backyards.
About halfway through training, he dropped out because of a knee injury. I soldiered on. After 16 weeks of prep, I felt ready, so I set out on my own—no aid stations or medals waiting at the finish line—and accomplished the trek to Annapolis, Maryland, and back in the middle of a snowstorm, with 84 laps in the community pool counting as my 1.2-mile swim.
Later on, I moved to Jackson, Wyoming, where my runs, swims, and bike rides would take place in the shadow of the Tetons. I decided to increase my training workload to try for a full-distance Ironman, also DIY, in Grand Teton National Park. I doubled everything from the 70.3 training block except for the weekend long runs. The schedule as written would have quickly had me running marathons the day after punishing bike rides that took half a day and marked my longest-ever distances in the saddle.
It wasn’t easy. Trail runs and lake swims easily eclipsed the distances I’d done for my high school cross country and swim teams, respectively. And the time was hard to schedule around my 9-to-5. I found a few encouraging partners to swim, ride, and bike with, but I did the majority of the sessions on my own.
The joy of training in pristine wilderness, as spring turned to summer, turned out to be solid motivation. After missing only a handful of workouts over 16 weeks, I felt ready.
I had done another solo half-Ironman to get a feel for the course, my gear, and my fitness level. The week before my target DIY attempt on August 8, I raced a short gravel triathlon with some friends in Steamboat Springs, Colorado, placing second in the first-timers category.
An ill-fated first attempt
The week of my taper, I relaxed with virtually no workouts. On the day of my attempt, unfortunately, a thick smoke from a West Coast wildfire filled the valley. The swim felt fine, and the bike ride was issue-free, but I could feel my lungs working overtime. By the time I started the run, I couldn’t fathom the marathon ahead of me. Temperatures crested at 80°F, and I was dipping my face and hands in every available stream.
Seven miles in, I started walking and, from there, it was all over. Doing an Ironman without any of the pressure of an organized event means it’s much easier to quit at any point. And the moment I FaceTimed my parents to fill them in, I knew I could just as easily come back and try again the following weekend. No pricey entrance fee or travel to make up. This is my backyard.
So I waited for the smoke to clear, made sure to do a more reasonable taper, and tried again the following weekend, with some of the nerves already shaken out.
Sure, these are luxuries I wouldn’t have had if I’d done a “real” Ironman. But it’s certainly in line with the ethos of these mountains: Sometimes it’s not your summit day. Goldman Sachs slashed its price target by more than half and still told clients to buy. What happened next turned a bad call into a case study in how a correct diagnosis can still destroy a portfolio.

FMC (NYSE:FMC | FMC Price Prediction) was already bleeding when Goldman Sachs (NYSE:GS) weighed in. The crop chemicals maker filed its Q3 2025 results on Oct. 29, 2025, with the stock at $25.68. Two sessions later it closed at $14.78.
On Nov. 3, 2025, Goldman cut its price target to $19 from $43 and kept its Buy rating. Since that Oct. 31 close, FMC has lost 58.04%. Meanwhile, SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) gained 10.8% over that period. Goldman took a cleaver to its target. The market’s cut went much deeper.
Why Goldman Kept Its Buy Rating
Goldman’s case had real logic behind it. The company beat EBITDA expectations in the third quarter of 2025. The trouble was pricing: generic competition in Latin America had turned out much worse than expected, and that pressure was spreading to FMC’s older, off-patent products. Goldman lowered its valuation to reflect that damage and still saw value in the shares despite the sharp target cut.
Goldman had the diagnosis right. It underestimated how far the damage would spread.
How Generic Pricing Pressure Swallowed the Thesis
The first blow landed on Feb. 4, 2026. Q4 revenue fell 11.5% to $1.083 billion, missing estimates. FMC took a $1.356 billion goodwill impairment, put its India business up for sale, saw Moody’s cut its credit to junk, and authorized a review of strategic options that included a possible sale of the company. Its flagship insecticide, Rynaxypyr, was facing generic competition after losing patent protection.

The number International Business Machines (IBM) shareholders are watching comes from one business: its software. You may think of IBM as a consulting and hardware company, but its growth question lies in software. Yet over the year to November 3, 2026, IBM stock lost 16.5%, while the S&P 500 returned 11.9%. IBM’s software growth sped up in fiscal Q3 2026 anyway, and that is the contradiction. So how fast is IBM’s software growing now, and how much of it is new?
IBM’s Software Speed-Up Came Mostly From New Business
Measured at constant currency, IBM’s software revenue grew 9% in fiscal Q3 2026. That was four points faster than in Q2, management said on the October 21 call. Its high-value annual recurring revenue base, software sales that repeat each year, grew 8% to $24.9 billion.
Some of a jump like that can be borrowed from the quarter before, and IBM did close about two-thirds of the large deals that slipped out of Q2. Management, however, put those deals at about a quarter of the speed-up and called about three-quarters of it net new business. Based on management’s own split, most of the gain was not catch-up.
Can IBM’s Software Growth Hold As Mainframe Software Cools?
Management said not all of that growth will hold. The company does not expect transaction processing, the software that runs on its mainframes, to keep growing at double digits, and said it could perhaps moderate from Q3 into Q4. So more of the growth has to come from the rest of IBM’s software, such as Red Hat, and so far Red Hat is holding up.
That matters because software license deals have already swung IBM’s software growth once. In fiscal Q2 2026, management said, a double-digit fall in transactional software sales, which make up about a fifth of its software business, cut software growth by 4 to 5 points. In Q3, those sales rose by double digits, mostly in transaction processing, which grew 10%.
Red Hat looks steadier. Its revenue grew 11% in fiscal Q3 2026, the same rate as the quarter before, and its bookings growth sped up to the high teens. OpenShift, a Red Hat product, is now a $2.4 billion annual recurring revenue business, growing more than 30%.
What Would Show IBM’s Software Growth Fading?
From the 9% alone, you cannot tell how much of IBM’s software growth will repeat. Part of it came from deals that slipped out of Q2, and the double-digit rise in mainframe software is the part management expects to fade. If the new business does not repeat, the speed-up was a one-quarter jump. If Red Hat does not grow into the gap, IBM’s software growth again swings with mainframe deals.
Management has said little about 2027 so far. When Red Hat’s bookings and 2027 came up on the October call, management declined to comment on 2027 growth. Later in the call, it gave only an early view that growth would speed back up to its model. It did say bookings growth of this kind usually turns into good revenue growth.
So far, management credits most of IBM’s software speed-up to new business, and Red Hat’s bookings are growing faster than they were. Since management expects mainframe software to cool, Red Hat’s ability to grow into the gap is the open question. IBM’s software growth, along with Red Hat’s part in it, is the number to watch when IBM reports in January 2027. Management has said it will put figures on 2027 then.

Somewhere along the way, I absorbed the idea that a runner’s body should look a certain way. When mine didn’t match that image, I started wondering if I wasn’t training hard enough, if I was doing something wrong, or if my body simply wasn’t responding the way it was supposed to.
As I approached race day, I thought about why I was holding myself to that standard in the first place, especially because I was running the New York City Marathon on behalf of Planned Parenthood of Greater New York, an organization whose work centers on bodily autonomy and compassionate care.
Why was I putting so much pressure on my body to look different when it was already doing something incredible? I realized training for a marathon isn’t just about building endurance; it can also mean confronting the expectations you place on yourself.

So many people have an idea of what a “runner’s body” is supposed to look like, particularly fed by what we see online. When you see the same body type represented over and over, it’s easy to start associating that appearance with athleticism. Salesforce's 50% stock declines are rare
Salesforce has been a public company since 2004. In its more than 22 years as a public company, its stock has dropped 50% or more from its all-time high on only three occasions:
- Oct. 7, 2008: Salesforce stock fell sharply, along with the broader market, as the financial crisis shook Wall Street. Salesforce stock ultimately declined by 70% before bottoming in November 2008.
- Sept. 1, 2022: Salesforce stock melted slowly throughout late 2021 and nearly all of 2022 during the latest bear market. After crossing the 50% threshold in September 2022, the stock bottomed in December 2022, down 59% from its all-time high, before recovering and setting new all-time highs in 2024.
- Feb. 23, 2026: Salesforce stock fell below the 50% mark in February 2026 as market participants fretted over whether software-as-a-service (SaaS) business models would withstand rapid innovations in the artificial intelligence (AI) sector.

In 2008, shares dropped another 39% before the bottom was truly in. In 2022, shares fell another 16%.

In his season-ending press conference, Cardinals president of baseball operations Chaim Bloom addressed several topics, from the team’s coaching staff to whether it will add pitching in the offseason to the progress of many of the team’s rookies this past season. But he created perhaps the most intrigue with his description of the team’s situation at third base, which he described as being a “long-term vacancy.”
Much of the Cardinals’ lineup looks mostly set for 2027, at least for now:
C: Leo Bernal
1B: Alec Burleson
2B: JJ Wetherholt
SS: Masyn Winn
LF: Joshua Baez
RF: Jordan Walker
DH: Ivan Herrera
That leaves center field and, yes, third base. So, with free agency now underway and the non-tender deadline looming on Nov. 20, here’s a look at five potential options for the Cardinals at third base for 2027.
The former top prospect: Nolan Gorman
This is probably the least likely name on the list. Given one more chance to win the third base job that was once thought to be his for the foreseeable future, Gorman struggled mightily in 2026, hitting .184 with just nine homers in 85 games. He was sent down to the Minors in June and stayed for two months to work on his swing, but he didn’t look appreciably better upon returning in late August, posting a .523 OPS in 73 plate appearances.
Gorman was a first-round pick by the Cardinals in 2018, and he’s been with the club for parts of five seasons, so he’s now due for a raise via arbitration in 2027. If the Cardinals can’t find a suitor willing to buy low on him, they could choose to non-tender Gorman, cutting him loose rather than offering him a contract for 2027. But the power stroke is still real, and this is a guy who had 27 homers as recently as 2023 … so maybe they give him one more chance?
The rookie: Blaze Jordan
Jordan was the player who was called up in June when Gorman was sent down, which was considered a surprise at the time because it was thought that Jordan wasn’t a good enough fielder to hold down third base on a regular basis. It turned out his defense was perfectly adequate, but the bat did not play as hoped. Jordan posted a .276 OBP, with only three homers and seven walks in 58 games.
That was a bit of a disappointment, considering he had a robust .921 OPS at Triple-A Memphis when he was called up. However, Jordan had been hitting a little better when he sustained a season-ending high ankle sprain on Aug. 27. Bloom, who drafted Jordan when he was with the Red Sox, clearly believes in him, and if Jordan is healthy, he might be the path of least resistance in the short term. But he’s going to have to hit a lot better if he wants to hold onto that job for long.
The utility guy: Thomas Saggese
Saggese got off to a very rough start in 2026 and was batting .184 when he was sent down in June. But when Jordan was injured in August, it was Saggese, not Gorman, who took advantage. He hit .279 with three homers and a .755 OPS over his final 25 games, which stood head and shoulders above anything else the Cardinals got at the position in 2026. He feels like a placeholder here -- one who could end up moving around the infield in a utility role -- but then again, he was a regular .300 hitter in the Minors and impressed many around the Cardinals in September.
It should be noted that Sagesse could have some competition even for that utility role.

Confluent, a subsidiary of IBM, has expanded its data streaming offerings with new functions aimed at supporting AI systems with real-time business context.
The company has made its Lightning Tables feature generally available on Amazon Web Services (AWS), finalising what it calls a five-pillar Data Streaming Platform (DSP).
Access deeper industry intelligence
Experience unmatched clarity with a single platform that combines unique data, AI, and human expertise.
This step adds query functionality to the existing capabilities to stream, connect, process and govern data under a unified approach for what Confluent terms the Streamhouse architecture.
The Streamhouse is intended to address a recurring challenge: as AI agents are introduced throughout enterprises, they must often make decisions based on fragmented, asynchronously updated data from a variety of systems.
This can result in decisions being made on outdated or conflicting information, potentially disrupting workflows.
The Streamhouse aims to resolve this by enabling the continuous capture, processing, governance and provision of current business information across systems, applications and analytics tools.
Confluent has illustrated the potential use case of an airline managing flight operations, where multiple systems can offer inconsistent views of aircraft locations, schedules and seat availability.
The Streamhouse model is designed to provide a constantly updated, shared view, allowing operational teams and AI decision-makers to respond in a timely and coordinated manner.
The architecture of the Streamhouse is built around three principles: it maintains continuously updated business information, it is designed for high availability and reliability, and it operates without requiring all data to be physically consolidated beforehand.
Rather than replacing existing data warehouses and lakehouses, it adds a real-time operational layer to support decision-making and actions.
At the centre of Confluent’s Data Streaming Platform is Apache Kafka, which streams business events.
The platform includes more than 150 managed and custom connectors for integrating enterprise data, batch execution features with Apache Flink, and tools for security and data governance such as schema and access policy controls.
The new query function offers several interfaces, including Confluent Tableflow for analytics, a Real-Time Context Engine for AI agents, and Lightning Tables for rapid SQL or API-based queries.
According to the company, Lightning Tables provides a read-only serving layer for data captured in Apache Kafka, enabling queries with reported latency between 10ms and 100ms and throughput exceeding 1,000 queries per second.
Features include multiple query interfaces, unified data governance, schema management and a machine learning feature store.
IBM Confluent and data general manager Shaun Clowes said: “The next era of enterprise AI will be won by the agents that know what’s happening in the business the moment they act. That’s what a Streamhouse can deliver.
“With Lightning Tables, our Data Streaming Platform gives each agent and application a live, governed view of the business. This means companies can act on fraud signals sooner, serve customers in the moment and run operations on what’s true now versus what was true yesterday.”

(Photo by Kent Becker, U.S. Geological Survey)
Missouri’s refusal to establish setback spacing requirements between concentrated animal feeding operations, to CAFOs. isn’t just a bureaucratic oversight — it’s a structural failure that guarantees cumulative pollution.
Our laws treat each CAFO as if it exists in isolation, but rural communities live with the reality of multiple industrial barns clustered together, all potentially draining into the same creeks, the same wells, and the same air column.
A single large CAFO can produce more manure than a small city. When two or three facilities operate side by side with no spacing requirements whatsoever, their waste streams can overlap. Yet the state reviews each permit separately instead of asking the obvious question: What happens when all that waste enters the same watershed? Rural Missouri already shows the consequences: increasing nitrate levels in private wells, persistent phosphorus pollution in streams, and industrial odors so strong that nearby residents cannot open their windows.
Missouri’s list of impaired waters has grown from 24 streams in 2002 to 549 in 2026. Of these, 215 were added after local control was removed in 2020 by SB391. Nearly half are impaired by e-coli or nutrients, potentially linked to CAFO waste and runoff.
The absence of setbacks is a likely accelerant. It allows industrial barns to stack like freight containers, concentrating millions of gallons of manure and wastewater in tight clusters. Regulators may insist each facility “meets its permit,” but permits don’t account for the combined load of multiple CAFOs operating in the same drainage area. Rural residents aren’t living next to one operation: they’re living next to the accumulated waste of an entire cluster.
A new trend is making the problem even worse: CAFOs are deliberately building barns just under the permit threshold to avoid regulation altogether. By staying a few animals below the number that triggers a state operation permit, operators side-step engineering reviews, public notice requirements, and even basic environmental safeguards. These “permit‑exempt” barns still produce enormous quantities of manure, yet they operate with virtually no oversight.

The Bank of England announced its first interest rate hike in over three years on Thursday, raising its key rate by 25 basis points to 4%.
The widely anticipated move marked the bank's first hike since Aug. 2023, and made it the last major central bank to embark on a tightening cycle since the U.S. and Israel went to war with Iran eight months ago.
The majority of the bank's Monetary Policy Committee voted for the quarter-point hike, with the motion passing by 8 votes to 1. The dissenting member voted to raise the bank's key interest rate by 50 basis points to 4.25%.
"The conflict in the Middle East is now in its ninth month," the MPC said in a statement Thursday. "Global energy prices have continued to rise from an already elevated level."
Policymakers said they now expected U.K. inflation to rise to "about 5%" by the middle of 2027.
"It is then projected to fall as the impact of rising energy prices on 12-month inflation rates fades, and still restrictive monetary policy bears down on inflation," they said.
Ahead of the decision being announced, markets had been pricing in more than a 99% chance of a rate hike, according to LSEG data. Traders were also pricing in a one-in-four chance of a further hike in December.
Iran war intensifies inflation pressure
Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey said in the November Monetary Policy Report that without "real progress towards settling the conflict in the Middle East... risks to energy prices, and so to inflation, are to the upside."
"Without news which softens the risks to inflationary pressures, I can see the argument for a further increase in rates and thereafter taking a more conditional approach, dependent on the evidence on energy prices and inflation dynamics," he said.
Data released earlier this month showed that the U.K.'s annual inflation rate jumped to 3.5% in September, driven by the surging cost of motor fuels.
As a net energy importer, the U.K. is particularly vulnerable to external energy shocks — such as the one caused this year by the Iran war.
The MPC's most hawkish member, Catherine L Mann, said she had voted for greater tightening than her peers because research pointed to "non-linear inflation risks."
"My recent votes to increase Bank Rate by 25 basis points represented a 'down payment' to lean against second-round effects, reinforce credibility, and uphold 'good policy'," she said in comments published in the MPC's policy statement.
"The economy has crossed the estimated statistical threshold into a high inflation-tight labour market regime where the asymmetric behavioural responses of households and firms support more robust second-round effects," Mann added. "A different research approach estimates that the economy may well have breached the policy credibility threshold, which worsens the policy trade-off... From a risk management and credibility perspective, a 50-basis point hike in Bank Rate is 'good policy'."
Yields on U.K. government bonds, known as gilts, had been rising before the policy announcement and continued to edge higher after the Bank of England's update. Aon plc, the re/insurance broker, announced the successful renewal of the Aon Client Treaty (ACT) facility.
From Jan. 1, 2027, the facility will enable 35% co-insurance on eligible business placed through Aon’s Global Broking Centre and on facultative reinsurance placed by Aon’s Reinsurance Solutions, up from 28.5%.
Strong support from market partners has matched growing client demand for committed capacity. Where permitted by local law and regulation, and subject to eligibility, the ACT Client Dividend of 1.5% will apply to the larger 35% share.
The facility is led by QBE and backed by Lloyd’s syndicates. Lloyd’s is rated “AA-” by S&P and “A+” by AM Best. Clients who choose to use ACT access its capacity on the same terms and pricing as the lead placement and may also be eligible for the dividend. Use of ACT is subject to client agreement, and Aon manages placements in line with its conflicts of interest framework.
The expansion for 2027 is particularly significant for facultative reinsurance, which ACT has supported since late 2025. Insurers placing large or complex individual risks through Aon can now access committed capacity, subject to eligibility criteria, for a larger portion of each placement.
Since its launch in 2016, ACT has placed more than $5 billion in gross written premium. Together with Aon Digital Placement Exchange, Aon Broker Copilot and Aon Claims Copilot, ACT reflects the firm’s continued investment in broking innovation. These capabilities are designed to streamline placement and claims and enhance the client experience.
“As the risks our clients face grow more complex and interconnected, efficient access to risk capital has never been more important,” said Joe Peiser, CEO Risk Capital, Aon, in a statement. “Increasing ACT to 35% gives clients greater efficiency and confidence when placing their risks. ACT is a clear demonstration of how Aon’s integrated Risk Capital approach delivers improved outcomes for clients.”
“ACT continues to evolve with what our clients need,” said Helene Madell, CEO of Global Broking Center, Aon. “Facultative reinsurance has quickly become one of the facility’s most important areas of growth and moving to 35% allows us to build on that momentum for clients.”

The Democratic midterm election sweep could result in changes in economic policies related to trade, spending priorities and artificial intelligence. But the biggest forces shaping the economy aren't going to change just because the party in power did.
Affordability pressures, heavy levels of government spending and growth that is dependent on the artificial-intelligence tailwind are likely to persist, economists say. And all of those factors pose risks to the economy.
"It's in a very kind of fragile place, and I don't know that it would take a lot to push the economy off the rails, and recession becomes a much greater risk," said Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics. "That isn't the case at the moment, but I don't think that's gone away."
Zandi said he had been worried before the election that the economy was under threat from inflation, an underwhelming labor market and geopolitical dangers, and remains concerned now.
Democrats romped to upset wins in not only House and Senate races but also governor and other state races. But economic and foreign policy is largely set in the executive branch, and President Donald Trump remains far apart from his Democratic adversaries, though he said Wednesday he anticipates working with them.
"I don't expect any change in economic policy. The Iran war, the tariffs and trade policy, the heavy-handed immigration policy, all are done under executive order. They're not legislatively driven," Zandi said.
"The president thought they were good policies before the election. I don't know why he'd change his mind after the election," he added. "So I think they will continue to be policies that restrain growth and add to inflationary pressures and interest rates."
Zandi sees the AI hyperscaler build-out as a key to economic growth, but also a source of potential peril.
"The risks are decidedly to the downside because the growth is so dependent on AI, and the AI growth effects are so dependent on the equity market, and the equity market is so dependent on the valuations," he said. "It just feels like kind of a very fragile place, and the labor market is not well functioning."
Local opposition to data centers was a fairly significant issue in the election, particularly for Democrats, according to CNBC polling, so that could be a further economic headwind, though the issue ranked below cost of living, corruption and several others.
Two economies
The election happened amid a dichotomy in economic views.
Topline numbers such as gross domestic product, consumer spending and the unemployment rate tell the story of an economy growing briskly while consumers spend and most Americans who want jobs are at work. GDP accelerated at a 3.4% annualized pace in the third quarter while consumer spending grew 3.8%. The unemployment rate is at 4.2% while layoffs are around their lowest level since 1969.

Failure to do so would block any bills that could improve the lives of Americans from becoming law and potentially lead to more shutdowns, since Congress must fund the government every year.
House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who will very likely become speaker in January, and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, will set the tone for that relationship, though committee chairs will play a significant role as well.

From hacked supermarket fridges and a record cryptocurrency theft at Binance to an emergency over flaws in widely used web software, companies worldwide are facing a wave of cyber threats executives say AI is accelerating and making more sophisticated.
The surge is straining IT departments, with staff working overnight to patch software vulnerabilities, prompting some companies to turn to and increase investment in AI-powered security tools to help manage the workload.
A cyberattack on European supermarkets on Monday, the second in three weeks in which hackers raised refrigerator and freezer temperatures, forcing retailers to discard millions of dollars’ worth of spoiled food, underscored the urgency.
Read more: European Supermarkets Rush to Patch Vulnerabilities After Region-Wide Fridge Hack
“It’s a never-ending game of cat and mouse, with very high stakes,” said Marnie Wilking, chief security officer at travel platform Booking.com.
“We shut down one route, and before we’ve even finished rolling out the fix, the bad guys have moved on to the next,” she said, adding that hundreds of engineers at the company were now building AI-powered defense systems.
Nearly 37,000 security flaws in software or computer systems were reported in the third quarter of 2026, tripling from a year earlier, according to the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures list, an international registry of disclosed security flaws.
“We’re seeing events of a magnitude every week, or even every couple of days, that used to be months apart,” Markus Noga, chief technology officer of German web hosting company Ionos, which serves seven million customers, told Reuters.
Ionos said it changed its security practices after seeing a spike in vulnerabilities in July, deploying AI-based monitoring systems to scan for threats and using AI-assisted tools to install patches on its systems around the clock.
“I’m kind of limited to what a nine-to-five office hours team can do and that’s no longer good enough,” Noga said.
Cyber Threats Drive Defensive Spending
Binance, hit by hackers who stole $6.3 billion worth of cryptocurrency, said it would increase investment in AI-enhanced detection systems. The Port of Rotterdam is working on an AI-powered “cyber shield,” while Siemens is testing advanced AI models for defensive security.
Dutch-based grocer Ahold Delhaize, which operates the Stop & Shop and Giant Food chains in the US, was hit by two hacks in the past month. The first, in mid-October, led to more than €200 million ($225 million) in sales losses and prompted a profit warning.
In that incident, Ahold took its websites and apps offline for a week after detecting an intrusion. This week, some of its stores in Belgium and Luxembourg were among those hit by cyberattacks on refrigerators across a dozen European countries.
“We’re adjusting to a new reality,” CFO Jolanda Poots-Bijl told Reuters, adding smaller firms were particularly exposed. At the same time, AI is a defensive tool, she said.
“AI also helps us to detect and to restore in a much faster way than we were ever able to do in the past,” she added.
McKinsey projects the global market for cybersecurity products and services sold by outside vendors will grow from $223 billion in 2025 to $346 billion by 2029.

European airlines suffered a second wave of bomb threats on Thursday that indiscriminately targeted companies from low-cost operator Wizz Air Holdings Plc to Finnish flag carrier Finnair Oyj, throwing air travel into disarray across a region already grappling with a series of security scares.
Among the flights affected was Aer Lingus Flight EI402 headed from Dublin to Rome, which was forced to make an emergency diversion to a military airfield in northern France. Finnair said two flights headed from Helsinki to Rome and Vienna got similar threats that turned out to be false.
Other carriers targeted included LOT Polish Airlines and Wizz, which was already at the receiving end of several threats earlier in the week. In the Czech Republic, police said they received bomb threats about four planes headed to Prague, and that the aircraft were searched after they touched down. Vienna’s main airport also received a warning about four flights, public broadcaster OFR reported.
Three Ryanair Holdings Plc flights headed to Sofia in Bulgaria from Madrid, Copenhagen and London were also targeted, a spokesperson for the Bulgarian ministry of transport said. Bulgarian MiG-29 fighter jets escorted the aircraft over Bulgaria’s airspace, the defense ministry said in a statement, and one of the flights was diverted to the city of Plovdiv.
Ryanair didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
“To have this in a coordinated way, I don’t think we’ve seen this before,” Ben Smith, the chief executive officer of Air France-KLM, said on a call with journalists to discuss third-quarter earnings. “It’s unfortunate and we hope it won’t give our consumers any reason to slow down or reduce their travel plan.”
No pattern has emerged around the spate of threats this week, either with the carriers drawn in or the routes that were affected. Bomb threats are rare events and almost always end up being hoaxes or the act of copycats. On average, there are more than 30,000 flights a day in Europe’s skies.
But the unusual rise in bomb threats comes at a time of heightened geopolitical tension and freak disruptions in Europe, including repeat hacking attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems and drone incursions into the territory.
Getting any illegal items on board is extremely difficult given how airports are ring-fenced and passenger screenings on the ground have become ever-more sophisticated.
As a result aircraft disasters involving a bomb are exceedingly rare. Notable incidents include Pan Am Flight 103 that exploded over Lockerbie in Scotland, killing all 259 people on board, in 1988, and a Russian passenger plane that was brought down by a an explosive device on board in Egypt’s Sinai peninsula in 2015, killing all 224 people on board.
Eurocontrol, the European coordinator of air traffic across the region, said it’s monitoring the situation and working closely with airlines, airports, air navigation service providers.
In Romania, authorities at Bucharest Otopeni Airport searched Wizz Flight WMT3064 after it landed from Milan with 182 passengers on board. The airport said it’s putting its safety protocol into practice, though other flights are still operating as usual.

The owner of the farm, Sunly, has insured Dagda and dozens of other large parks in Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Poland worth €600 million ($670 million) in case of any spillover from the war in Ukraine. The Tallinn-based company wanted to protect its assets and reassure its investors, who have been more careful about placing their money in the region.
“We see this as a real business risk,” said Peeter Raudsik, Sunly’s head of regulation. “Several big banks are demanding terrorism and sabotage insurance as the standard.”
From an apartment building in Romania to a parked car in Lithuania, drones from the war in Ukraine have increasingly been inflicting damage along NATO’s eastern flank this year. The heightened risk is now spawning a small, but growing area of the insurance business.
Many insurers in the region, particularly in the Baltics and Poland, have begun offering political violence or war risk cover. Incidents linked to Russia’s war in Ukraine are often followed by a spike in inquiries from businesses and homeowners nervous about protecting their property.
“We have a bit of dark humor in the insurance industry: We say that the best advertisement for insurance is a neighbor’s house on fire,” said Simonas Lisauskas, chief executive officer of Lietuvos Draudimas, the largest insurer in Lithuania. “Following events like these, we definitely observe a surge in client interest.”
Standard policies usually have a conflict exemption clause. In a high-profile case in July, the UK’s High Court decided that insurers were not liable for damages from the Nord Stream gas pipeline explosion in 2022 because they were a “consequence of war” and therefore exempt.
Critical national infrastructure — such as power plants, airports, data centers and utilities — have been among the biggest entities seeking more comprehensive cover. Then there are manufacturers, shopping centers and logistics warehouses. Additionally, homeowners, hotels, churches and educational institutions — including college Vilniaus Kolegija — have taken out policies.
Lietuvos Draudimas has signed more than 100 insurance contracts with businesses since May, said Lisauskas. One of them was Swedish telecommunications operator Telia, which last month insured its Lithuanian infrastructure, including data centers, for up to €50 million. The terms weren’t disclosed.
The Vilnius and Riga airports are also assessing new options for insurance against drones and geopolitical risks. So is a major Baltic seaport that declined to be identified publicly. A spokesperson for Riga Airport said the policy it currently holds covers risks related to terrorism and sabotage.
